1:1.t: Sosthenes may be the synagogue leader of Acts 18:17.

1:20.t: "Teacher of the law": the KJV's "scribe". "Philosopher": the KJV's "disputer".

4:4.t: "My conscience is clear": the KJV's "I know nothing by myself", which in 1611 meant "I know nothing against myself".

4:9.t: "At the end of the procession": like captives led last in a Roman victory parade, condemned to die in the arena.

4:13.t: "Scum ... garbage": the KJV's "filth ... offscouring", the dirt scraped off and thrown away.

4:15.t: "Guardians": the KJV's "instructers"; Greek paidagogos, the slave who looked after a child (Galatians 3:24).

5:7.t: "For us": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words.
"Our Passover lamb": the Passover lamb was killed and all yeast removed from the house (Exodus 12:15-21). Christ's death calls His people to clean out sin.

5:9.t: A letter of Paul to the Corinthians written before this one has not survived.

5:13.t: A quotation of Deuteronomy 17:7 and similar verses.

6:20.t: "And with your spirit, which belong to God": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words.
"Bought at a price": the language of buying a slave's freedom. Compare 7:23 and Romans 3:24.

7:5.t: "Fasting and": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words.

7:10.t: Jesus' teaching on divorce: see Mark 10:2-12.

7:15.t: "Not bound": many take this to mean the believer is free to remarry; others, only free to separate.

7:25.t: "Virgins": unmarried people, especially young women not yet married.

7:26.t: "The present crisis": the KJV's "the present distress", perhaps persecution or famine, or the troubles of the last days.

7:36.t: These verses are difficult. The KJV, followed here, takes them as a father deciding whether to give his daughter in marriage. Many modern Bibles take them as a man deciding whether to marry his fiancee.

8:6.t: "All things came ... through whom all things came": compare John 1:3.
"One God, the Father ... one Lord, Jesus Christ": Paul expands the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4) to include Jesus within the one God's identity.

9:5.t: "A believing wife": the KJV's "a sister, a wife". "The Lord's brothers": Christians differ on whether they were Mary's later children, Joseph's children from an earlier marriage, or cousins; see Matthew 12:46.

9:20.t: Some manuscripts add "though I myself am not under the law"; the KJV does not have these words.

9:25.t: The Isthmian Games were held near Corinth every two years. The winner's crown was a wreath of pine or celery, which soon withered.

9:27.t: "Disqualified": the KJV's "a castaway"; Greek adokimos, rejected after testing.

10:1.t: See Exodus 13:21-22, 14:22-29, 16:4-35 and 17:6. Jewish tradition told of a rock that followed Israel through the wilderness.

10:8.t: See Numbers 25:1-9, which gives 24,000, perhaps including those killed by the judges.

10:9.t: "Test Christ": the KJV's reading; some manuscripts read "test the Lord". See Numbers 21:4-9.

10:25.t: "Meat market": the KJV's "shambles". Much of the meat sold had first been offered in pagan temples.

10:28.t: "For 'The earth is the Lord's, and everything in it'": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not repeat these words here.

11:4.t: This passage reflects customs of dress and hair in the first-century Greek and Roman world. Christians today differ on how far the head covering is a binding practice and how far the underlying principles of honor and order apply in other forms.

11:10.t: "Authority over her own head": the KJV's "power on her head", meaning a covering as a sign of authority. "Because of the angels": perhaps because angels are present in worship (compare Psalm 138:1).

11:19.t: "Differences": the KJV's "heresies"; Greek hairesis, factions. The word first meant a party or school of thought; only later did "heresy" come to mean false teaching. See Acts 24:14.

11:24.t: "Take, eat ... broken": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have "Take, eat" or "broken".

"In remembrance" (Greek anamnesis): more than recalling a past event; at Passover Israel retold the Exodus as their own story, and the Lord's Supper makes Jesus' saving death present to those who share it (see Luke 22:19). "The new covenant in My blood": the KJV's "the new testament". Diatheke can mean a will, but here it translates the Hebrew berit, covenant, the new covenant promised in Jeremiah 31:31-34 (see Matthew 26:28).

11:29.t: "In an unworthy manner": the KJV's "unworthily"; many early manuscripts do not have these words in this verse. "Of the Lord": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read only "the body".

"Discerning the body" (Greek diakrinon to soma): recognizing the Lord's body. Many understand this as recognizing Christ's presence in the bread; others as recognizing the church as His body, which the Corinthians were dishonoring by humiliating the poor (11:21-22).

11:30.t: "Fallen asleep": died. The New Testament often speaks of believers' death as sleep, because they will be raised. See Acts 7:60.

12:28.t: "Guidance": the KJV's "governments", the gift of leadership or administration.

13:3.t: "To be burned": the KJV's reading; some early manuscripts read "that I may boast".

13:12.t: "In a mirror": the KJV's "through a glass". Ancient mirrors were polished metal and gave a dim, imperfect image.

14:2.t: "In a tongue": the KJV's "in an unknown tongue". The KJV printed "unknown" in italics as a supplied word; the Greek has only "in a tongue". Also 14:4, 14:13, 14:14, 14:19, 14:27.

14:16.t: "An inquirer": the KJV's "the unlearned"; Greek idiotes, an outsider or someone not yet instructed.

14:34.t: In some manuscripts these verses come after verse 40. Christians differ on how to apply them: as a lasting rule that women should not speak in church, as a rule for a particular situation of disruptive questions, or as limited to the weighing of prophecies (14:29). Paul has already assumed that women pray and prophesy in worship (11:5).

14:38.t: "Let them be ignorant": the KJV's reading; some early manuscripts read "they will be ignored".

15:7.t: James, the brother of the Lord (Galatians 1:19).

15:29.t: "Baptized for the dead": this practice is not mentioned elsewhere, and its meaning is uncertain. Paul mentions it without approving it, as evidence that even those who practice it believe in the resurrection.

15:32.t: "Fought wild beasts": perhaps a figure for fierce opponents. The quotation is Isaiah 22:13.

15:33.t: A quotation from the Greek poet Menander.

15:47.t: "The Lord from heaven": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "the second man is of heaven".

15:49.t: "We shall bear": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "let us bear".

15:54.t: Quotations of Isaiah 25:8 and Hosea 13:14. "O grave": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "O death" again.

16:1.t: The collection was for the poor believers in Jerusalem (Romans 15:25-28).

16:13.t: "Be courageous": the KJV's "quit you like men", act like men, be brave.

16:21.t: Paul dictated his letters to a scribe and added a final greeting in his own hand to show they were genuine (Galatians 6:11, 2 Thessalonians 3:17).

16:22.t: "Let that person be cursed! Come, Lord!": the KJV's "let him be Anathema Maranatha". Anathema is Greek for "devoted to destruction, cursed"; Maranatha is Aramaic, "Come, Lord!" or "Our Lord has come". Early Christians used it as a prayer (compare Revelation 22:20).
"Love" (Greek phileo): here the word for warm personal affection, rather than agapao, committed love; see John 21:15-17.

16:24.t: "Amen": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have it.

1:18.t: "Foolishness" (Greek moria): the source of "moron". To the ancient world a crucified Messiah was absurd and shameful; crucifixion was for slaves and rebels. "Those who are perishing ... us who are being saved": present tenses; salvation is a process as well as a past event.

1:23.t: "Stumbling block" (Greek skandalon): a snare or obstacle that trips someone up, causing offense or a fall; see Matthew 13:21.

2:6.t: "Mature" (Greek teleioi): the KJV's "perfect", meaning complete, mature, whole, not sinless. See Matthew 5:48.

2:14.t: "The person without the Spirit ... the person with the Spirit" (Greek psychikos ... pneumatikos): the KJV's "the natural man ... he that is spiritual". Psychikos means living by merely natural human life (psyche); pneumatikos means living by God's Spirit (pneuma).

3:1.t: "Worldly" (Greek sarkinos, sarkikos): the KJV's "carnal", fleshly: living by human nature apart from God's Spirit. See Romans 7:14.

3:13.t: "The Day": the day of the Lord's return and judgment (1:8).

3:15.t: "As one escaping through the flames": the picture is of a builder whose work is destroyed in a fire but who escapes. Roman Catholic teaching has seen in this verse support for purgatory; Protestants have generally read it as the testing of believers' works at the final judgment.

3:16.t: "You yourselves are God's temple" (Greek naos): "you" is plural; the church together is the dwelling place of God's Spirit. In 6:19 Paul applies the same picture to each believer's body.

4:1.t: "Servants ... those entrusted" (Greek hyperetas ... oikonomous): the KJV's "ministers ... stewards". An oikonomos managed a household or estate for its owner.

5:5.t: "Hand this man over to Satan": put him out of the church's fellowship into the world where Satan rules, so that he might repent. "The destruction of the flesh": his sinful nature, or bodily suffering. The aim is his salvation.

6:9.t: "Men who have sex with men" (Greek malakoi ... arsenokoitai): the KJV's "effeminate ... abusers of themselves with mankind". Malakos means soft, often used of the passive partner in male sexual relations; arsenokoites, apparently formed from the Greek of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13, means a man who lies with a male. Readers differ on how precisely these terms apply today. Most churches through history have taken such texts as teaching that sexual relations between people of the same sex are contrary to God's design; some recent interpreters argue that Paul had in view particular practices of his day, such as exploitation or idolatrous cults (see the note at Romans 1:26-27).

6:11.t: "Washed ... sanctified ... justified": three pictures of what God has done. The past tense stresses that it is already accomplished.

6:12.t: "I have the right to do anything" ... "Food for the stomach": Paul appears to quote slogans used in Corinth, then answers them.

6:19.t: "Your bodies are temples" (Greek to soma hymon naos): "body" is singular and "your" plural, perhaps "your body (each of you) is a temple". Compare 3:16, where the church together is God's temple.

7:1.t: "It is good for a man not to have sexual relations with a woman": many take this as a saying from the Corinthians' letter, which Paul then qualifies. The KJV's "not to touch a woman" was a polite expression for sexual relations.

7:14.t: "Sanctified" (Greek hegiastai): set apart. The believing spouse brings the household within God's sphere of holiness; it does not mean the unbeliever is saved (7:16).

7:31.t: "Form" (Greek schema): the KJV's "fashion", the outward shape of the present world order, which is passing away.

8:1.t: "Knowledge" (Greek gnosis): some in Corinth prided themselves on special knowledge. "Love" (Greek agape): the KJV's "charity". See chapter 13. "Builds up" (Greek oikodomei): the KJV's "edifieth", builds a house.

8:9.t: "Your rights" (Greek exousia): the KJV's "this liberty", the freedom or authority to act.

9:12.t: "Right" (Greek exousia): the freedom or authority to act; see 8:9. Paul gave up his right to be paid in order not to hinder the gospel.

9:18.t: "Right" (Greek exousia): the freedom or authority to act; see 8:9. Paul gave up his right to be paid in order not to hinder the gospel.

9:21.t: "Under Christ's law" (Greek ennomos Christou): bound to Christ's law of love (compare Galatians 6:2).

10:2.t: "Baptized into Moses": Israel's passing through the sea under the cloud was a picture of baptism, uniting them with Moses as their leader.

10:13.t: "Temptation" (Greek peirasmos): both temptation and testing; the same word covers being tempted to sin and being tested to prove faithful. See Matthew 4:1. "A way out" (Greek ekbasis): an exit, a way through.

10:16.t: "Participation" (Greek koinonia): the KJV's "communion", sharing in common, partnership, participation. See Acts 2:42. Sharing in the Lord's Supper unites believers with Christ and with one another (10:17). Christians differ on how Christ is present in the Supper: as a real presence in the bread and wine, as a spiritual presence, or as a memorial sign (see Matthew 26:26).

10:20.t: "Demons" (Greek daimonia): the KJV's "devils". A daimonion is a demon, an evil spirit; "devil" (diabolos) is reserved for Satan. See Matthew 4:24. The idols themselves are nothing, but evil spiritual powers stand behind idol worship (Deuteronomy 32:17).

11:3.t: "Head" (Greek kephale): readers differ on whether it means "authority over" or "source, origin" (as in the head of a river), or both. Paul's argument in 11:8-12 draws on creation and also stresses mutual dependence "in the Lord".

12:1.t: "Gifts of the Spirit" (Greek pneumatika): the KJV's "spiritual gifts", literally "spiritual things". In 12:4 Paul calls them charismata, gifts of grace.

12:10.t: "Tongues" (Greek glossai): the word means both the tongue and a language. At Pentecost they were real languages the hearers understood (see Acts 2:3-4); here they need interpretation (14:2-5, 27-28).

13:1.t: "Love" (Greek agape): the KJV's "charity", from the Latin caritas, which in 1611 meant self-giving love, not giving to the poor. Agape is not mainly a feeling but committed goodwill that seeks another's good, even an enemy's. See Matthew 5:43-44. In this chapter Paul describes agape by what it does.

13:10.t: "Completeness" (Greek to teleion): the KJV's "that which is perfect". Readers understand this as Christ's return and the age to come, the completion of the New Testament, or the church's maturity. Verse 12 ("face to face") points most naturally to the end.

13:13.t: "Faith, hope and love": the three lasting virtues (compare 1 Thessalonians 1:3, 5:8). Love is greatest because it endures into eternity, when faith becomes sight and hope is fulfilled.

14:3.t: "Strengthening, encouraging and comfort" (Greek oikodome, paraklesis, paramythia): the KJV's "edification, and exhortation, and comfort", the purpose of prophecy.

15:3.t: "What I received I passed on to you": the language of handing down a fixed tradition. Verses 3-5 are among the earliest Christian statements of faith, likely received by Paul within a few years of the resurrection.

15:20.t: "Firstfruits" (Greek aparche): the first part of the harvest, the pledge of the rest; see Romans 8:23. Christ's resurrection is the first sheaf of the harvest that guarantees the rest.

15:23.t: "Firstfruits" (Greek aparche): the first part of the harvest, the pledge of the rest; see Romans 8:23. Christ's resurrection is the first sheaf of the harvest that guarantees the rest.

15:44.t: "Natural body ... spiritual body" (Greek soma psychikon ... soma pneumatikon): psychikos means living by merely natural human life (psyche); pneumatikos means living by God's Spirit (pneuma); see 2:14-15. A "spiritual body" is not a body made of spirit, but a real body fully animated and ruled by God's Spirit, like Christ's risen body.

15:52.t: "In the twinkling of an eye" (Greek en rhipe ophthalmou): in an instant. "The last trumpet": compare 1 Thessalonians 4:16.

15:55.t: "Grave" (Greek hades): the realm of the dead (Hebrew Sheol), not Gehenna, the place of final judgment; see Matthew 11:23.

16:2.t: "On the first day of every week": Sunday, the day of Jesus' resurrection, already the day Christians met (Acts 20:7).
